Q: How do I use SFTP without SSH? A:

SFTP happens to be used by SSH servers but it's a well-developed protocol that works well on its own. The sftp-server developed by OpenSSH has no dependency on an SSH server; sftp-server uses standard input/output. (Other SFTP servers are similar.)

It is trivial to share a filesystem via SFTP, similar to what you might do with NFS but without the need for root access. I'll use socat as the daemon for this ad-hoc example, but xinetd would make a more permanent solution. The location of sftp-server is from my Ubuntu installation of the openssh-sftp-server package.

On the server:

$ mkdir shared_to_the_world
$ cd shared_to_the_world
$ socat tcp-listen:1234,reuseaddr,fork exec:/usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server

On the client:

$ mkdir /tmp/sftp_test
$ sshfs -o reconnect,ssh_command="nc my_sftp_server_address 1234 --" : /tmp/sftp_test
$ cd /tmp/sftp_test

Now your client (and anyone else's!) can seamlessly work with the files in the shared directory on the server. Both read and write are enabled, so be careful.

Consider using socat listen's "bind" and "range" options to limit the access to your server.

update:

Newer versions of nc do not honor the "--" option to signal the end of options to nc. A bunch of ssh-specific options are tacked on to the command, causing nc to fail.

Gemini helped me with the following replacement for the client command:

sshfs -o ssh_command="sh -c exec\$IFS'nc'\$IFS'localhost'\$IFS'1234'" : /tmp/sftp_test

Q: Store long-lived password securely in PBEKeySpec or a Key Store A:

What you want is not possible without involving specialized hardware.

To define things clearly:

  1. You have an application which is in a state that it can apply a cryptographic operation without further input that you want to protect (i.e. the admin did have to provide some input on app start, but the app is currently running and the intent is that it can do stuff without the admin providing any further input at this point).
  2. It is running on a device which is under complete control of a malicious actor. Or, to reduce the severity of the compromise: A malicious actor has full access to a point-in-time memory dump.

Then...

  1. You've lost the game. The malicious actor can perform unauthorized actions. And no amount of code can possibly fix that.

What would help is hardened hardware: A near guarantee that it is extremely difficult to obtain a memory dump. This is provided by e.g. apple's T2 chip or lots of modern windows hardware's TPM chip. However:

  • TPM chips in particular have been a bevy of compromises.
  • It is not all that easy to interact with these chips. If you really want to, it usually requires programming in the 'platform native' language, not java.
  • These chips usually have a limited set of operations they can 'do'; you can't program them. You haven't explained what operation you are doing for which you want to try to 'protect' the admin key, but if it's not something the TPM/T2 chip is capable of doing you cant program that chip to be capable of it.

Alternative 1: Dump the responsibility onto the admin user.

This is hardware a user is entering a password into. If the hardware is compromised than nothing you could possibly do will save this admin. They have typed their password into hardware under control of a malicious actor: The game is, obviously, lost, completely. The solution isn't to try to protect against such a situation with your software. It's instead to tell the user not to use compromised hardware.

Equate 'malicious user can access a complete memory dump' to 'malicious actor has taken control of the hardware'. The gap between those two scenarios is not very large.

In other words, inform the admin user that they are responsible for ensuring a full memory dump of your app is not made available to untrusted parties or software.

Alternative 2: Password-every-time-mode

Make the storing of the password an optional feature; the admin user can choose to enter a password -every time- the operation is needed. You will need to do some work on the java side to ensure your implementation of this concept actually can cash the cheque you're writing with such an option: You must ensure the password is only ever present in a char array and is not ever turned into a java.lang.String object, and that, immediately after the operation is complete, you zero out that char array. This should be 'safe' (i.e. a memory dump made after zeroing out the array will not expose the secret). If you've ensured this (for example by reading the source of any libraries you use to double check they don't turn things into strings or otherwise move it into non-wipable heap structures), you can at least claim that the admin user of your software merely needs to ensure that no memory dump made in the middle of the operation, immediately after the admin user enters the password ever makes it to untrusted entities.

Personal opinion: This a virtually meaningless upgrade to the threat model. But, you may hold a different opinion on this notion.

Q: Duplicated code-gen on clang for non-defaulted destructor in templated class with shared_ptr A:

In the C++ standard,

An implicitly-declared default constructor is an inline public member of its class.

The explicit equivalent would be inline ~A() = default. Adding this makes the builds identical.

In particular, it causes Clang codegen to annotate the destructors with inlinehint, so LLVM inlines ~B() into B::operator=(B&&), which doesn't inline into the variant<B>::operator=(variant<B>&&) visitor, which inlines into the variant<...>::operator=(variant<...>&&) dispatcher, which doesn't inline through to reset, where it would realize it only needs to assign A<0> and the others are dead code.

Q: Is fetching std::chrono::steady_clock inside a critical section necessary to theoretically align C++ happens-before with real-time order? A:

You either have:

  • "clear", "empty" (the more natural case)
  • "ok", "clear" (the "inverted" execution)

Over a noticeable physical time gap (such as 1 hour), physical reality dictates t1 < t2.

Your timing seems huge, but you can also imagine a very slow machine with instructions which can take years to execute.

Waiting 1 year, 1h, 1s, 1ms is similar from the abstract machine.

And once you consider more "practical" cases, you are no longer in the theory.

Q: The precision of printf with specifier "%g" A:

The exact representation in memory of the decimal 3122.55 is a binary fraction with a 53 bits mantissa.

printf("%a\n", value);     // output 0x1.865199999999ap+11

And the exact conversion back to a decimal is:

printf("%.45f\n", value);  // output 3122.550000000000181898940354585647583007812500000

If you cut that number at 17 digits you get:

printf("%.17g\n", value);  // output 3122.5500000000002

And at 16 digits, all the trailing digits are 0 and could safely be erased (which the g format does automatically by default) to get:

printf("%.16g\n", value);  // output 3122.55

That is why you get back the original decimal number.

Q: View query results from a PL/SQL block without PUT_LINE, RETURN_RESULTS, or CREATE? A:

The issue is that SELECT QTest(v_ID) FROM DUAL returns the ref cursor as one opaque column, not an expanded rowset which only works when a client explicitly binds a REF CURSOR OUT param, not from a plain SELECT.

Since you can't create objects, skip ref cursors entirely and use dbms_xmlgen + XMLTABLE to turn your dynamic SQL into XML, then shred it back into a normal rowset in the same statement. If you are using oracle-12.1, just build the SQL string directly inside getxmltype() instead.

Example

SELECT x.*
FROM XMLTable('/ROWSET/ROW'
    PASSING dbms_xmlgen.getxmltype('SELECT Value1, Value2 FROM MyTable WHERE ID = $ID')
    COLUMNS Value1 VARCHAR2(100) PATH 'VALUE1', Value2 VARCHAR2(100) PATH 'VALUE2') x

Q: Determining a segmentation fault occurring in this loop A:

I agree with Daniel, you need to be checking your return values and pointers.

I also agree that you need to do a better job blocking and formatting your code. Supposing that you are the only one that ever reads it, in a couple of weeks even you will have forgotten enough that you won't be able to follow it.

Towards Matthews point, you could try deleting everything starting with the line:

printf ("here 5ai\n");

Of course, only bother with this after checking the file pointer.

Another crazy idea would be stepping through it with a debugger. I know it's hard to use a debugger when you have such great debugging options as the printf statement, but sometimes a debugger can be a huge time saver (for example, when you keep getting segfault). Also, learning how to use the debugger for the platform you are developing on is one of the things that separates good coders from the pack of average hacks. (FYI, you could even try looking at your core in the debugger and maybe see exactly where the problem is. (Hint: if you don't have a core file try 'man ulimit'.))

If you are going to insist on using printf as your only means of debug, then call flush right after each use.
